At its most common, animus means a strong feeling of hostility, dislike, or ill will directed at a specific person, group, or thing. It is not just mild dislike — it carries a sense of deep-seated, often personal antagonism. Think of it as a charged, negative attitude that someone carries toward a specific target.

"The judge was removed from the case because of her obvious animus toward the defendant."

Here, the judge doesn't just dislike the defendant — she has a strong, underlying prejudice against them that could cloud her judgment.

A key quality of animus is that it tends to be targeted and persistent. You don't feel animus toward a stranger you bumped into once. It's more like a settled, ongoing hostility — the kind that builds over time or stems from a deep-rooted bias.
How It Differs from Similar Words

You might wonder: isn't this just hatred? Or animosity? Here's how to tell them apart cleanly:

  • Hatred is raw and emotional — it's what you feel in your gut.
  • Animosity is very close to animus, but animosity suggests an active, visible conflict or tension between two parties. It's more mutual. Two rivals have animosity between them.
  • Animus is more internal and one-directional. One person or group harbors animus toward another. It's the underlying attitude — the prejudice or bias living beneath the surface — that drives hostile behavior.

So animus is best thought of as the root cause — the hidden engine — of hostile or discriminatory behavior. It's the "why" behind someone acting unfairly or aggressively toward another.

"His animus toward immigrants was evident in every policy he proposed."

Here, animus explains the motivation for his actions, not just the actions themselves.

In law, animus is used very precisely to mean intention or motive — the mental state or purpose behind an action. Lawyers and judges use it to ask: what was this person's underlying intention?

For example:

  • Did this person discriminate because of genuine animus (hostility/prejudice) toward a protected group?
  • Was an act done with animus furandi (intention to steal)?

In this legal sense, proving animus is often crucial — because the same action can be innocent or criminal depending on the intention behind it. Courts look for animus as evidence that a person acted out of bias or malice, not just by accident or coincidence.

The Swiss psychologist Carl Jung gave animus a very specific technical meaning in his theory of the human psyche, and this is a well-known secondary meaning of the word.

According to Jung, every person has both conscious and unconscious dimensions to their personality. He observed that the human unconscious contains traits that are opposite to one's outward, social self (what he called the "persona"). He named these unconscious opposite forces:

  • Anima — the unconscious feminine dimension present in men.
  • Animus — the unconscious masculine dimension present in women.

So for Jung, the animus is the internal masculine energy living in a woman's unconscious mind. It doesn't mean a woman is masculine outwardly — rather, it refers to qualities like assertiveness, logic, drive, and authority that exist in a deeper, hidden layer of her psyche.

Jung believed that becoming a whole, psychologically mature person requires acknowledging and integrating this hidden side of yourself — not suppressing it. A woman who ignores her animus, for example, might find those energies expressing themselves in unhealthy or uncontrolled ways (such as sudden, irrational outbursts of aggressiveness or rigid, inflexible thinking).

This Jungian meaning is separate from the everyday meaning of hostility, and you'll mainly encounter it in psychology, literature, and philosophy.

In a broader, somewhat literary or formal sense, animus can also refer to the central spirit, intention, or driving force behind something — not necessarily hostile, but the motivating essence of something.

"The animus of the entire movement was a desire for justice."

Here, animus means the soul or driving spirit of something. This usage is less common in everyday conversation but appears in more elevated writing and academic discourse. You can think of it as the animating force — the life or purpose that breathes energy into a cause, work, or effort.

SituationWhat "animus" means
Everyday languageStrong, targeted hostility or deep-seated prejudice toward someone or something
Legal languageThe intention or motive behind an action, especially a biased or malicious one
Jungian psychologyThe unconscious masculine side of a woman's psyche
Formal/literaryThe driving spirit, motivation, or animating force behind something

If you remember nothing else: animus is the deep, underlying hostility or prejudice someone holds toward a specific person or group. It's not casual dislike. It's the kind of animosity that motivates behavior — often unfair, discriminatory, or aggressive behavior. When someone acts with animus, there's a personal, charged, targeted ill will behind it.

That one core meaning will serve you correctly in the vast majority of situations where you encounter this word.
